strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis of the discrepancy between the objectives of regular ReID and MOT: the observation that per-sequence targets occupy only a limited region of the general ReID feature space and are highly similar is intuitive and supported by feature visualizations (Figs. 1, 3, 4).

Training-free, closed-form approach based on Fisher Linear Discriminant that can be plugged into existing feature-based trackers without modifying other components, which is practical and reproducible.

Extensive evaluation across four diverse benchmarks (DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, TAO) with consistent improvements over the ReID-only baseline, e.g., DanceTrack HOTA 50.6 -> 61.2 and MOT17 HOTA 61.5 -> 63.5.
Demonstrated zero-shot transfer capability using multiple MASA variants (Table 4), showing the method generalizes across different ReID feature sources without retraining.

Thorough ablations on the historical queue length T, temporal-shift coefficient lambda_0, integration coefficient alpha, and a comparison against PCA as an alternative dimensionality-reduction baseline, which helps disentangle the effect of the proposed components.
Honest discussion of limitations (missing position information, CPU-based eigendecomposition, inability to learn the projection), which is appropriate and adds credibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism is a direct application of the classical Fisher Linear Discriminant (1936) to per-sequence trajectory features. The additional contributions (temporal-shifted centroid, linear knowledge integration) are simple modifications, so the paper reads more as an empirical study than a new algorithmic contribution.

Fairness of the SOTA comparison is questionable. The base tracker is deliberately stripped down to ReID-only with a single-stage Hungarian matching, so gains over motion- or hybrid-based trackers partly reflect the simplified testbed and detection pipeline rather than the proposed transformation. The unusually large margin on SportsMOT (7.2 HOTA over DiffMOT) raises the possibility of detection/config differences.

Cold-start and small-sample regimes are not adequately addressed. FLD relies on per-sequence class statistics, and the projection is unstable when few trajectories exist or early in a sequence; the paper does not analyze behavior in these regimes, and the D' = min(C-1, D) constraint means the projection is heavily restricted when C is small.

The knowledge-integration rationale (generalization vs. specialization, alpha = 0.9 favoring the projected space) is somewhat hand-wavy, and the paper does not deeply justify why a simple convex combination is the right form or whether the trade-off is robust across datasets.

The central claim that the original ReID space is 'wasteful' because targets occupy a limited subspace is largely supported qualitatively; there is no quantitative measure of subspace occupancy or intra-sequence similarity to substantiate the argument.

Computational overhead is significant (22.7 FPS on DanceTrack with CPU eigendecomposition), and although the authors acknowledge this, the practical impact for real-time MOT is not fully resolved within the paper.

strengths: The core observation is well-motivated and non-trivial: the paper correctly identifies that ReID features are trained for general discrimination across identities while MOT association requires discriminating highly similar targets within a single sequence, and it supports this with clear visualizations (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 4) showing that per-sequence features occupy a limited region of the original space and are ambiguous for similar targets.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and practical. Using Fisher Linear Discriminant with a closed-form solution (eigen-decomposition of S_W^-1 S_B) over historical trajectory features as pseudo-classes is an elegant way to obtain a sequence-adaptive, discriminative subspace without any additional training, which is a genuine practical advantage.

The paper is technically careful in adapting FLD to the online MOT setting, introducing two MOT-specific modifications (Temporal-Shifted Trajectory Centroid with dynamic weighting lambda_t = lambda_0^t' and Knowledge Integration that fuses the projected and original spaces via alpha) and ablating each component thoroughly.

The experimental evidence is broad and reasonably convincing: four benchmarks (DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, TAO), comparison against motion-based, hybrid-based, and ReID-based SOTA, plus a zero-shot transfer study (Table 4) with four different MASA encoders. The improvements on DanceTrack (50.6 -> 58.6 HOTA) and SportsMOT are substantial, and the zero-shot gains are consistent across encoders.

The ablation studies are informative and fair. Table 5 directly contrasts FLD with PCA to show the choice of objective matters, and Tables 6-8 justify the history length T, the temporal weighting lambda_0, and the fusion coefficient alpha. The use of a single-stage, ReID-only tracker as a controlled baseline isolates the effect of the proposed module.

The paper is clearly written, the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) is easy to follow, and the Limitations section honestly discusses the absence of position cues and the CPU eigen-decomposition bottleneck, which aids reproducibility and scientific honesty.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely an application of a classical technique (Fisher Linear Discriminant) plus standard engineering choices (EMA, weighted centroid, weighted fusion of two similarity spaces). While the framing and MOT-specific adaptation are valuable, the methodological novelty is moderate and may not meet the bar of a top-tier venue on its own.

The comparison is not entirely apples-to-apples. The baseline (FastReID-MOT) deliberately excludes position/motion information, while the state-of-the-art methods compared against in Tables 1-3 rely heavily on motion cues. The claim that a feature-only tracker becomes 'competitive or superior' to SOTA therefore partly reflects the artificial restriction of the baseline rather than a fully fair comparison; the paper does acknowledge this, but the framing in the abstract/intro could overstate the result.

Reliance on FLD introduces practical concerns that are not fully analyzed: the projection dimension is min(C-1, D) and depends on the number of currently active trajectories, which changes continuously. The paper does not study the stability or variance of the per-frame projection when the number of classes is small or changes abruptly (e.g., new targets appearing), which is a real robustness question for a sequence-adaptive method.

The reported inference speed (22.7 FPS) and the CPU-bound eigen-decomposition are a meaningful practical limitation. The paper defers the engineering fix (GPU eigenvalue solver) to future work, but since the projection must be recomputed as trajectories evolve, the actual overhead and its scaling with target count are not quantified.

No statistical significance or multi-seed variance is reported for the main results, and the improvements on MOT17 and TAO are relatively small, suggesting the method mainly helps in similar-appearance scenarios. A clearer delineation of when the method helps (and when it does not) would strengthen the claims.

The FLD-derived projection is conditioned on previously tracked targets, so it can be corrupted by early ID mis-associations; the paper mentions this risk when motivating the knowledge integration but does not empirically characterize the failure mode or its propagation.

strengths: The core idea is clearly articulated and intuitive: exploiting the mismatch between ReID's generic goal and MOT's within-sequence discrimination goal, and using historical trajectory features as class conditions for a Fisher Linear Discriminant projection (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2). The motivation (Fig. 1a/b) is well illustrated.

The method is training-free and drops into existing feature-based trackers without retraining the ReID model, which is a practically attractive property; the zero-shot experiments on MASA/SAM backbones (Table 4) show consistent gains across four visual encoders and three benchmarks, supporting the generality of the claim.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough: projection choice (FLD vs. PCA vs. no projection, Table 5), history length T (Table 6), temporal-shift coefficient λ0 (Table 7), and integration coefficient α (Table 8) are all examined, and the PCA comparison and Fig. 3/Fig. 4 visualizations help justify why FLD is preferred.

The paper includes a limitations section (Appendix C) that honestly acknowledges the omission of positional cues and the single-stage tracker design, and discusses inference cost (22.7 FPS) and the CPU-bound eigenvalue bottleneck, which is useful for readers.

Results on SportsMOT (Table 3) show a genuine and sizeable margin over motion-based/hybrid competitors using the same ReID model (e.g., +7.2 HOTA over DiffMOT), which is a nontrivial empirical finding.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and the framing overstates it. The central mechanism is the application of Fisher Linear Discriminant / LDA — a classical, closed-form technique from 1936 — to ReID features, with the only customization being that trajectories are treated as classes. The temporal-shifted centroid is an exponential-weighting heuristic (Eq. 9) and knowledge integration is a convex combination of two cosine similarities (Eq. 10). The paper itself calls the approach 'straightforward'; the incremental nature of the contribution relative to the strong claims in the abstract ('superior tracking performance compared to state-of-the-art') is not adequately supported.

The headline SOTA claim is not substantiated by the tables. On DanceTrack (Table 1) HAT-FastReID-MOT reaches 58.6 HOTA while DiffMOT reaches 62.3 and C-BIoU 60.6; on MOT17 (Table 2) HAT-FastReID-MOT is 63.5 versus C-BIoU 64.1 and DiffMOT 64.5. The method is competitive, not superior, and the 'surpasses state-of-the-art' statement in the abstract and Sec. 4.3 is a stretch. The gains are large only relative to the authors' own deliberately minimal single-stage baseline (FastReID-MOT), which weakens the strength of the comparison.

There is an unresolved circular dependency: the FLD projection is computed from historical trajectory features, which are themselves produced by association decisions that depend on the projection. Early association errors or ID misallocations can corrupt the class statistics and the projection matrix. The paper acknowledges this risk (Sec. 3.4) but does not analyze, bound, or mitigate it — no experiment measures sensitivity to association noise. Additionally, the projection matrix and its dimensionality (D' = min(C-1, D)) change every frame as trajectories are born/die, and the stability of this non-stationary subspace is never examined.

The computational cost is a serious practical limitation that is largely relegated to Appendix B.1. Computing an eigendecomposition on a 2048-D scatter matrix per sequence per frame on CPU yields 22.7 FPS, and the authors' own analysis attributes the bottleneck to this operation. For a method whose selling point is a lightweight, training-free add-on, the absence of a cost/accuracy trade-off table in the main paper and the lack of an end-to-end efficiency comparison against the cited SOTA methods is a substantive omission.

Baseline and comparison fairness: the 'Naïve ReID-Based Tracker' (Appendix A.1) deliberately excludes positional information and multi-stage cascades, so the reported improvements conflate the proposed transformation with the choice of a weak baseline. The PCA comparison in Table 5 is also questionable — PCA with D' = N_obj-1 / N_id-1 components is a straw-man configuration, and a stronger dimensionality-reduction or metric-learning baseline would have made the case more convincing. No comparison to other online feature-adaptation or test-time-adaptation approaches is provided.

Presentation quality issues: in Table 3, two rows share the label 'HAT-FastReID-MOT†' with different numbers (79.3 and 80.8), which is a labeling error that undermines confidence in the reported results; Table 1 also uses inconsistent bold/duplicated conventions. Combined with awkward phrasing, the manuscript reads as under-polished.

The contribution type is not declared. Under the Algorithms/General category that I applied, the algorithmic novelty (a per-frame FLD re-projection plus two hand-tuned scalars) is thin, and no theoretical analysis (e.g., on the stability or generalization of the online projection) is offered to compensate. If recast as an Applied/Systems paper, the evidence is stronger, but the overclaimed SOTA framing and the missing efficiency analysis would still need to be addressed.

strengths: Clear, well-articulated problem framing: the authors correctly identify that MOT association is a closed-set discrimination problem within a single sequence, whereas off-the-shelf ReID features are optimized for open-set retrieval, and they support this claim with a quantitative analysis (the δ1000 discriminability metric vs. AssA correlation on DanceTrack in Fig. 2a and SportsMOT in Fig. 6a), which is a useful diagnostic contribution in its own right.

The proposed solution is simple, training-free, and has a closed-form solution (FLD/LDA with historical tracklet identities used as pseudo-labels), making it easy to plug into existing trackers. The paper demonstrates this portability concretely: gains on a ReID-only tracker (FastReID-MOT), on hybrid trackers (ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Hybrid-SORT), and on MASA across four different backbones (Tables 1-3), which is broader evidence than many MOT papers provide.

The empirical gains on the target benchmarks are substantial: DanceTrack HOTA improves from 50.6 to 61.2 (AssA 31.6 to 46.0) for the ReID-only tracker, and SportsMOT from 67.3 to 81.2/78.9, making the ReID-only tracker competitive with, and in some cases better than, hybrid and end-to-end trackers. These are large, consistent improvements that directly support the paper's thesis.

The ablation study is unusually thorough and includes genuinely informative controls: comparison against PCA with matched output dimensionality (Table 5) isolates the effect of label-awareness from mere dimensionality reduction, and the supervised-FLD baseline (Table 9) shows that an FLD trained on labeled videos from other sequences does not transfer, which directly supports the sequence-specificity argument and is a nice piece of evidence for the paper's core motivation.

The paper is candid about limitations and negative results: marginal gains on MOT17/MOT20 (Sec. 5.3, Appendix B.1), the limitations of the method on hybrid and end-to-end trackers (Appendix C), the runtime overhead (Appendix B.5), and even unsuccessful technical attempts (Appendix D). This honesty improves the credibility of the claims and is helpful to the community.
Clarity is good overall; the method is easy to follow, the pipeline figure (Fig. 3) is informative, and the incremental ablation design (Appendix A.5) makes each component's contribution traceable.
weaknesses: Novelty is the main concern. The core idea - treating historical track identities as pseudo-labels and learning a discriminative projection (LDA/FLD) for appearance features online - has close precedents in the tracking literature (online/incremental discriminative appearance learning, LDA-based metric learning, adaptive affinity methods such as ref. [22], and the closed-set observation already made in ref. [64]). The claim of being 'the first work to provide an intuitive explanation, a systematic analysis, and a practical solution' overstates the novelty; the contribution is better characterized as a clean systematization plus strong empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The primary baseline (FastReID-MOT) is constructed by the authors rather than taken from published results. Although they state that it is grid-searched to maximize performance, a self-built baseline makes it difficult for a reader to verify that the reported gains are not partly attributable to an under-tuned comparison point, which weakens the headline numbers.

The method's computational cost is significant (22.7 FPS vs 46.5 FPS for the baseline, as reported in Appendix B.5), and the FLD step relies on a generalized eigendecomposition (scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W)) of a 2048-dimensional scatter matrix with a small number of samples per class. Numerical issues around the singularity of S_W (regularization/shrinkage) and the fact that the projected dimension d' = min(C-1, d) is very small (on the order of the number of trajectories) are not discussed, which is a technical gap for reproducibility.

Comparison with recent literature is incomplete. The authors acknowledge in Appendix D that they omit recent trackers; on DanceTrack the proposed method (HAT-Hybrid-SORT-ReID 66.9 HOTA) remains below recent end-to-end methods (MOTIP 69.6, SambaMOTR 67.2), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is confined to SportsMOT and to the ReID-only tracker category. This should be stated more precisely in the main text.

The gains are strongly dataset-dependent: large on DanceTrack and SportsMOT but marginal on MOT17/MOT20 (about 2.0 HOTA), and the paper offers only a post-hoc explanation (higher inherent discriminability in pedestrian datasets, Fig. 4/5). There is also no variance analysis across runs/seeds and no statistical significance testing, which matters given the small margins on MOT17/MOT20.

Hyperparameters (T, λ0, α) are tuned per dataset, and the claim that the default settings transfer well across datasets would be more convincing with a clearer separation between tuned and default configurations in the main tables (currently only indicated with a dagger). The knowledge-integration fusion is a cost-matrix-level heuristic whose optimal α = 0.9 places 90% of the weight on the transformed space, which somewhat undercuts the stated motivation of retaining the original space for robustness; a more principled fusion or an analysis of error propagation from erroneous historical pseudo-labels is missing.

The temporal weighting (λ_t = λ0^{t-t'} with λ0 = 0.9, T = 60) effectively discards almost all older frames (weight of the oldest frame ≈ 0.9^60 ≈ 0.002), so the 'history-aware' component is largely a recency weighting; the paper does not analyze how this interacts with the FLD's need for sufficient samples per class.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated core insight: MOT is a closed-set, sequence-specific discrimination problem rather than an open-set retrieval problem, which is supported by a quantitative correlation analysis (Fig. 2a, Fig. 6a) linking ReID discriminability (δ1000) to association accuracy. This gives the work a principled foundation beyond ad-hoc tuning.

The proposed history-aware FLD transformation is training-free and plug-and-play, and the authors demonstrate consistent gains across a wide range of settings: ReID-based trackers (FastReID-MOT), hybrid trackers (ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Hybrid-SORT), and multiple visual backbones via MASA (Tab. 1-4). The SportsMOT result (78.1 HOTA, 69.9 AssA) establishing new SOTA for an appearance-only tracker is notable.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough and well-designed. The 'supervised vs. history-aware' experiment (Tab. 9) is particularly valuable, showing that a FLD trained on labeled data from other videos does not transfer well, which directly supports the claim that the optimal subspace is sequence-specific rather than simply an artifact of introducing FLD.

The paper honestly reports and analyzes negative/marginal results (MOT17, MOT20, TAO) rather than hiding them, and provides a plausible explanation (high inherent target discriminability in pedestrian datasets, Fig. 4/5) that is consistent with the paper's central hypothesis.

Good scientific hygiene: separate discussion of limitations (Appendix C), hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix D), inference-speed analysis with root-cause diagnosis, and even unsuccessful technical attempts, which is useful to the community.
Clear writing, well-structured pipeline figure (Fig. 3), and appropriate attribution of datasets and methods.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the central mechanism is a fairly direct application of classical Fisher Linear Discriminant / LDA (a nearly 90-year-old method) with a history-aware labeling scheme. The novelty lies mainly in the framing and the two practical adaptations (temporal weighting, similarity-score fusion) rather than in a new algorithmic principle. The paper would be stronger if it more explicitly positioned the delta over prior appearance-customization works [6, 8, 22, 30, 52] beyond the general 'closed-set vs. open-set' argument.

Non-trivial computational overhead: inference drops from 46.5 FPS to 22.7 FPS on DanceTrack (Appendix B.5), with the generalized eigenvalue solve on CPU being the bottleneck. While near-real-time, this roughly halves throughput and may limit applicability in crowded/high-target-density scenarios, which the authors partially acknowledge.

Performance gains on the standard pedestrian benchmarks are modest (e.g., only +2.0 HOTA on MOT17, Tab. 4/10), and the method cannot be applied to end-to-end trackers. This narrows the practical scope and the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim, which is concentrated on DanceTrack/SportsMOT.

The comparison omits several recent strong trackers by the authors' own admission (Appendix D); since many of these depend on motion cues or heavy hyperparameter tuning, the claimed SOTA on SportsMOT may not hold against all current methods. The head-to-head advantage is demonstrated primarily against a self-constructed baseline (FastReID-MOT), which—although carefully tuned—makes the strongest gains less externally verifiable.

The 'knowledge integration' fusion (Eq. 8) combines two similarity matrices at the score level rather than in feature space; the paper justifies this by dimensionality mismatch but does not explore alternative fusion strategies (e.g., feature-space concatenation or learned weighting), leaving a natural design question open.

Some claims (e.g., 'first work to provide an intuitive explanation, a systematic analysis, and a practical solution') are somewhat strong given the existence of related appearance-customization works; the framing as a fundamentally new problem class risks overstating the conceptual gap.

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation: the paper correctly identifies that MOT is a closed-set, sequence-specific discrimination task whereas ReID is an open-set retrieval task, and uses this mismatch as the basis for feature transformation. Section 3.2 and Fig. 2 provide quantitative evidence (δ1000 vs. AssA correlation) supporting the hypothesis.

The proposed method is conceptually simple, training-free, and plug-and-play: it can be inserted into existing ReID-based and hybrid trackers (Tables 1, 2, 3) with consistent gains, which is a practically attractive property.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements are reported: e.g., HAT-FastReID-MOT improves DanceTrack HOTA from 50.6 to 58.6 (61.2 with tuning) and SportsMOT HOTA from 67.3 to 78.1, and consistent gains are demonstrated across four visual backbones (Table 3) and across hybrid trackers such as Hybrid-SORT and OC-SORT.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough (Tables 5–9), including a valuable comparison against a supervised FLD trained on ground-truth labels, which supports the claim that sequence-specific history supervision matters more than large-scale supervised training.

The paper is generally well-written, the method is described in sufficient detail (Sec. 4, Appendix A), and public pretrained weights are used, aiding reproducibility. Limitations (hybrid trackers, end-to-end methods, MOT17 marginal gains, inference speed) are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core mechanism is a direct application of the classic Fisher Linear Discriminant (1936) using historical trajectory assignments as pseudo-labels. The observation that MOT is a closed-set discrimination problem is reasonable but not new, and the remaining components (temporal weighting of centroids, similarity-matrix fusion) are simple heuristics rather than methodological advances. The paper reads more like an engineering recipe than a new algorithm.

The comparison protocol is potentially unfair. The main quantitative claims rest on a self-constructed baseline (FastReID-MOT) that is not publicly available, and the largest reported gains (Tables 1 and 2) are relative to that baseline. Although the method is also applied to existing trackers (Hybrid-SORT, OC-SORT), the gains there are noticeably smaller, which raises the question of how much of the headline improvement is attributable to the proposed method versus an under-tuned baseline.

Inference cost is non-trivial and under-addressed. FPS drops from 46.5 to 22.7 (Sec. B.5), roughly a 2× slowdown due to per-sequence generalized eigenvalue decomposition on CPU. While the authors argue this is an engineering issue, real-time MOT is a key application scenario and a halving of throughput is a substantive practical limitation, not a mere detail.

The paper claims state-of-the-art on SportsMOT, but the strongest competing methods are largely from ~2 years ago (e.g., MOTIP, MeMOTR, SambaMOTR). The authors themselves acknowledge omitting recent hybrid trackers, so the SOTA claim is weaker than presented, and the framing of the contribution would benefit from being more measured.

Generalization to the most standard MOT benchmark is weak: on MOT17 (Tab. 4/10) the gain is only ~2.0 HOTA over the baseline and does not surpass strong hybrid trackers (DiffMOT). The explanation (high intrinsic discriminability of pedestrians) is plausible but also indicates that the method's benefit is dataset-dependent and limited to visually homogeneous scenarios.

Dependence on historical pseudo-labels is a real concern: the method implicitly trusts past assignments, including erroneous ones, to build the projection. The 'knowledge integration' fusion with the original space mitigates but does not resolve this, and no analysis of robustness under high ID-switch rates or long occlusions is provided.
